results.query: Why did the Roman Empire eventually collapse?
results.response: The fall of the Roman Empire was a complex process that unfolded over many centuries, caused by a combination of internal decay and external pressures. The Western Roman Empire formally ended in 476 CE when the Germanic chieftain Odoacer deposed the last Roman emperor, Romulus Augustulus. Key causes include: (1) Political instability and corruption. The Roman Empire experienced a crisis in the 3rd century CE with over 20 emperors in 50 years, many of whom were assassinated. The Praetorian Guard frequently murdered emperors and auctioned the throne. The division of the empire into Eastern and Western halves under Diocletian weakened central authority. (2) Economic decline. Heavy taxation to support the military and bureaucracy crippled the economy. Inflation was rampant as emperors debased the currency. Trade routes became disrupted, and the empire faced a chronic trade deficit. (3) Military problems. The empire became over-reliant on barbarian mercenaries who had little loyalty to Rome. The army faced constant pressure from Germanic tribes (Visigoths, Vandals, Ostrogoths) along the Rhine and Danube frontiers. The Battle of Adrianople in 378 CE was a devastating defeat. (4) Barbarian invasions. The Huns pushed Germanic tribes into Roman territory. The Visigoths sacked Rome in 410 CE, and the Vandals did so again in 455 CE. Rome was eventually besieged multiple times. (5) Social decay. Traditional Roman values declined, and there was a widening gap between the wealthy elite and the poor masses. The institution of slavery stifled technological innovation. (6) The split between the Eastern and Western Empires created divergent paths, with the Eastern (Byzantine) Empire centered on Constantinople surviving for another thousand years. The Eastern Empire had greater wealth, more defensible borders, and better strategic leadership.

The academic dress of the United Kingdom and Ireland has a long history and has influenced the academic dress of Canada and the United States and beyond. The academic square cap was invented in the UK as well as the hood which developed from the lay dress of the medieval period. Irish academic dress is virtually the same as that in the United Kingdom given the common history and proximity of each other. Many other Commonwealth countries also follow British cuts and design of academic dress, most notably Australia and New Zealand though some are beginning to evolve away from British cuts such as Canada, where the University of Toronto has slowly introduced American gowns that close at the front. There's a distinction between different types of academic dress. Most recently, gowns, hoods and caps are categorised into their shape and patterns by what may be known as the Groves classification system, which is based on Nicholas Groves's document, Hood and Gown Patterns. This lists the various styles or patterns of academic dress and assigns them a code or a Groves Classification Number. For example, the Cambridge BA style gown is designated [b2] and a hood in the Cambridge full-shape is designated [f1], etc. Because the universities are free to design their own academicals using a wide range of available gown, hood and cap patterns, colours and materials at their and the robemaker's disposal, the academicals of two given universities rarely clash with each other. The Burgon Society was founded in 2000 to promote the study of academic dress. It has publications and activities to do with academic dress and published an updated version of Shaw's book on British and Irish academical dress in 2012, with a second volume covering non-degree awarding bodies published in 2014. Gown
The modern gown is derived from the roba worn under the cappa clausa, a garment resembling a long black cape. In early medieval times, all students at the universities were in at least minor orders, and were required to wear the cappa or other clerical dress, and restricted to clothes of black or other dark colour. The gowns most commonly worn, that of the clerical type gowns of Bachelor of Arts (BA) and Master of Arts (MA), are substantially the same throughout the English-speaking world. Both are traditionally made of black cloth, (although occasionally the gown is dyed in one of the university's colours) and have the material at the back of the gown gathered into a yoke. The more traditional is the curved yoke, whilst the square or straight yoke is used more in modern times. Another type of gown is called the lay type gown, which is similar to the MA gown in that it has long closed sleeves, but doesn't have a yoke. Instead, there's a flap collar with the gathers underneath it. Thus it's less voluminous than the clerical type gown. This gown is often used for the dress of officers and graduates of some degrees (especially at Oxford and Durham). In the Commonwealth, gowns are worn open, while in the United States it has become common for gowns to close at the front, as did the original roba. For a $300,000 loan at 6.5% for 30 years: monthly rate = 0.065/12 = 0.00542, number of payments = 360, monthly payment = about $1,896. But your actual monthly payment will be higher because it also includes property taxes (typically 0.5-2% of home value annually) and homeowners insurance (typically $500-$2,000 per year). If your down payment is less than 20%, you'll also pay private mortgage insurance (PMI). Use an online mortgage calculator for the most accurate numbers  --  they include taxes, insurance, and PMI automatically.

results.query: Why do we have leap years every four years?
results.response: A leap year is a calendar year that contains an additional day compared to a common year. The 366th day is added to keep the calendar year synchronised with the astronomical year or seasonal year. Since astronomical events and seasons don't repeat in a whole number of days, calendars that have a constant number of days each year will unavoidably drift over time with respect to the seasons. By inserting an additional day -- a leap day -- or an additional month -- a leap month -- into some years but not others, the drift between a civilisation's dating system and the physical properties of the Solar System can be avoided.
